source_batch.unit_label: ABFM Module B unit 2 (courseware unit 8): financial and operating leverages

facts.statement: Financial leverage (courseware): financial leverage is the use of borrowed funds to enhance the return to equity shareholders (earnings per share) without bringing in more equity; the assumption is that the cost of borrowing is less than the value added by the assets bought with it. It is limited by two factors: as the debt to equity ratio rises the lender will lend at a higher rate or not at all, and the additional surplus may fall below the cost of borrowing, reducing EPS; owners therefore impose a prudential limit. It is a double-edged sword: it can enhance return on equity and, beyond an optimal level, harm it. Measures: debt to assets (total debt / total assets), debt to equity (total debt / total equity), debt to EBITDA, the equity multiplier (total assets / total equity) from Du Pont analysis, and interest coverage (EBIT / interest expense).

Degree of financial leverage (courseware): DFL is the ratio of the percentage change in EPS to the percentage change in EBIT; because tax rate and number of shares are constant, the percentage change in EPS equals the percentage change in EBT, and because interest is a fixed amount a change in EBIT equals the change in EBT, which gives DFL = EBIT / EBT (EBIT less interest is EBT). Worked example: EBIT 2,00,000 and interest 1,00,000 give EBT 1,00,000 and DFL of 2 times. A positive DFL greater than 1 means financial leverage is relevant: the firm operates above break-even and EBIT and EPS move in the same direction; with no fixed interest DFL is 1; at break-even (EBIT equals interest) EBT is nil and DFL is undefined; below break-even EBT is negative and DFL is negative. Illustration with interest of 20,000 on EBIT of 1,00,000 rising to 1,50,000: EPS rises from 4 to 6.5, a 62.5 per cent rise against a 50 per cent rise in EBIT, so DFL is 1.25.

Operating leverage and DOL (courseware): operating leverage arises from fixed operating costs (other than interest); a business with high fixed costs is sensitive to a drop in sales volume, whereas one with low fixed costs and low contribution is in profit even if sales are low. DOL is the percentage change in EBIT divided by the percentage change in sales, which simplifies to contribution divided by EBIT (contribution is sales less variable cost; EBIT is contribution less fixed cost). Worked examples: 1,000 units at Rs 50 with variable cost Rs 30 and fixed cost Rs 15,000 give contribution Rs 20,000, EBIT Rs 5,000 and DOL of 4; with no fixed cost DOL is 1 (a 50 per cent rise in sales raises EBIT 50 per cent); with fixed cost a 50 per cent rise in sales can raise EBIT 100 per cent (DOL 2); when EBIT is nil DOL is undefined; a negative DOL means the firm operates below break-even and EBIT is negative. DOL falls as sales rise above break-even (Z Ltd with break-even of 2,000 units: DOL is 5 at 2,500 units and 3 at 3,000 units).

Break-even and leverage; combined leverage (courseware): break-even point (units) = fixed cost / contribution per unit; the firm with high operating leverage has a higher break-even point and higher fixed cost, and a firm with lower fixed cost has lower operating leverage and a lower break-even point. Combined (total) leverage combines operating and financial leverage: DTL is the percentage change in EBT (or EPS) divided by the percentage change in sales, DTL = DFL x DOL = (EBIT / EBT) x (contribution / EBIT) = contribution / EBT. Example: sales Rs 10,00,000, variable cost Rs 7,00,000, fixed cost Rs 2,00,000 and interest Rs 50,000: contribution 3,00,000, EBIT 1,00,000, EBT 50,000; DOL 3, DFL 2 and DTL 6. A 10 per cent change in sales then moves EBT by about 60 per cent. Fixed operating costs and fixed financial costs together act as the pivot that magnifies the sensitivity of owners' returns to a change in units sold.

payload.title: Financial leverage: borrowing to lift earnings per share
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Financial leverage** means using **borrowed funds** to raise **EPS** without raising more equity. It pays only if the **assets bought with the debt earn more than the debt costs**.

It is **limited** because as **debt rises** lenders charge **more** or refuse, and the extra surplus may drop **below** the cost of borrowing, so EPS can **fall**. It is a **double-edged sword**.

**Measures:** **debt to assets**, **debt to equity**, **debt to EBITDA**, the **equity multiplier** (total assets over total equity) and **interest coverage** (EBIT over interest).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: There is no single standard measure; each shows leverage from a different angle.

self_check.prompt_text: When does financial leverage raise EPS?
self_check.expected_takeaway: When the assets bought with borrowed money earn more than the cost of the borrowing.

payload.title: Degree of financial leverage
payload.core_explanation_md:
**DFL = % change in EPS / % change in EBIT**, which simplifies to **EBIT / EBT** because interest is a **fixed amount**.

**Reading it:** DFL **above 1** means a **given % change in EBIT produces a larger % change in EPS**. With **no interest**, DFL is **1**. At **break-even** (EBIT equals interest) EBT is nil and DFL is **undefined**; **below** it DFL is **negative**.

assumptions: Tax rate and number of shares are constant
common_errors: Treating a company below break-even as having a meaningful positive DFL

payload.expanded_explanation_md: A DFL of 1.5 means a 10 per cent rise in EBIT lifts EPS by about 15 per cent, and a 10 per cent fall cuts it by about 15 per cent.

self_check.prompt_text: What is DFL when a firm has no interest burden?

payload.title: Degree of operating leverage
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Operating leverage** comes from **fixed operating costs** (other than interest).

**DOL = % change in EBIT / % change in sales = contribution / EBIT**, where **contribution = sales less variable cost** and **EBIT = contribution less fixed cost**.

With **no fixed cost**, DOL is **1**. The **higher the fixed cost**, the **higher the DOL**, and DOL **falls** as sales move **further above break-even**. At **EBIT of nil** DOL is **undefined**.

assumptions: Fixed cost and price and variable cost per unit are constant over the range
common_errors: Using sales instead of contribution in the numerator

payload.expanded_explanation_md: A firm with high fixed costs and low variable costs gains sharply when sales rise and loses sharply when they fall.

self_check.prompt_text: What happens to DOL as sales rise further above break-even?

payload.title: Break-even, fixed cost and operating leverage
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Break-even units = fixed cost / contribution per unit.**

| Firm | Fixed cost | Break-even point | Operating leverage |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **High leverage** | High | **Higher** | **Higher** |
| **Low leverage** | Lower | **Lower** | **Lower** |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: In the courseware example Product A has the higher fixed cost and contribution per unit and a DOL of 4, while Product B has a lower DOL, about 2.67.

self_check.prompt_text: Why does higher fixed cost raise the break-even point?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because more contribution is needed before fixed cost is covered.

payload.title: Combined (total) leverage
payload.core_explanation_md:
**DTL = DOL x DFL = contribution / EBT.**

It measures how a **% change in sales** is magnified into a **% change in EBT or EPS** by **both** the fixed operating costs and the fixed financial costs together.

For example, a DTL of **6** means a **10 per cent** change in sales changes EBT by about **60 per cent**.

assumptions: Fixed operating cost and fixed interest
common_errors: Adding DOL and DFL instead of multiplying
Using EBIT in place of EBT in the denominator

payload.expanded_explanation_md: EBIT cancels in the product, which is why contribution over EBT gives the combined leverage directly.

self_check.prompt_text: How is DTL related to DOL and DFL?

payload.title: Worked example: DOL, DFL and DTL for one firm
payload.core_explanation_md: A firm has sales of Rs 30,00,000, variable cost of 60 per cent of sales and fixed operating cost of Rs 6,00,000. It pays interest of Rs 2,00,000. Find its DOL, DFL and DTL.

worked_steps.description: Contribution is sales less variable cost.
EBIT is contribution less fixed cost.
DTL = DOL x DFL = contribution / EBT.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: DOL is 2, DFL is 1.5 and DTL is 3 (times)

self_check.prompt_text: By how much does EPS rise if sales rise 10 per cent?
self_check.expected_takeaway: By about 30 per cent, since DTL is 3: EBIT rises 20 per cent and EBT 30 per cent.

payload.stem_md: A firm sells 8,000 units at Rs 75 with variable cost of Rs 45 per unit and fixed cost of Rs 1,50,000. What is its contribution (Rs)?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Contribution per unit is 75 - 45 = Rs 30; for 8,000 units it is 30 x 8,000 = Rs 2,40,000.

payload.stem_md: For the same firm (8,000 units, price Rs 75, variable cost Rs 45, fixed cost Rs 1,50,000), what is the degree of operating leverage (to 2 decimal places)?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Contribution is Rs 2,40,000 and EBIT is 2,40,000 - 1,50,000 = Rs 90,000, so DOL = 2,40,000 / 90,000 = 2.67 times.

payload.stem_md: How many units must the same firm sell to break even?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Break-even = fixed cost / contribution per unit = 1,50,000 / 30 = 5,000 units.

payload.stem_md: Using the degree of operating leverage of 2.67, by about what percentage will the firm's EBIT fall if sales volume falls by 10 per cent (to 1 decimal place)?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Percentage change in EBIT = DOL x percentage change in sales = 2.67 x 10 = 26.7 per cent. Direct check: 7,200 units give contribution 2,16,000 and EBIT 66,000, a fall of 24,000 on 90,000, which is 26.7 per cent.

payload.stem_md: A firm has EBIT of Rs 6,00,000 and interest of Rs 2,00,000. What is its degree of financial leverage (to 1 decimal place)?
The same firm has 60,000 shares and pays tax at 40 per cent. EBIT rises by 20 per cent to Rs 7,20,000 with interest unchanged. What is the new EPS (Rs, to 1 decimal place)?
payload.correct_explanation_md: EBT = 7,20,000 - 2,00,000 = 5,20,000; tax at 40 per cent leaves 3,12,000; EPS = 3,12,000 / 60,000 = Rs 5.2. Earlier EPS was 4, so EPS rose 30 per cent for a 20 per cent rise in EBIT, matching DFL of 1.5.

unresolved: This unit is the courseware's account of leverage analysis, standard financial management. No regulatory source applies and none was consulted.

The courseware derives DFL = EBIT / EBT by assuming that interest is fixed and that a change in EBIT equals the change in EBT; it ignores preference dividends. The unit teaches this standard form and states the assumption.

The courseware's Illustration 2 for financial leverage uses a profit-volume ratio of 27.55 per cent and bonds "of Rs 1,000 each" in a way that does not affect the ratio; the illustration is not reproduced, and new figures are used in every numerical item.
